title: Alkenes
learningObjective: know that alkenes contain the functional group >C=C<; know the general formula for alkenes; explain why alkenes are classified as unsaturated hydrocarbons; understand how to draw the structural and displayed formulae for alkenes with up to four carbon atoms in the molecule, and name the unbranched-chain isomers knowledge of cis/trans or E/Z notation is not required; describe the reactions of alkenes with bromine to produce dibromoalkanes; describe how bromine water can be used to distinguish between an alkane and an alkene

sections.title: Alkenes
sections.markdown:
Cracking (u4:c23) does more than top up the petrol supply — it also
splits large [[alkane]] molecules into smaller ones that carry a
very different bonding feature: a carbon-carbon **double bond**.
That one structural difference defines a whole new family of
[[hydrocarbon]]s, the **[[alkene]]s**, and it makes them far more
reactive than the alkanes you have just studied (u4:c24). Where an
alkane chain is chemically quiet, an alkene's double bond is a
ready-made handle that other molecules can grab — and the entire
chemistry of this chapter hangs off that handle.

The double bond has a formal name in organic chemistry: it is the
**[[functional-group]]** of the family, written >C=C< to show the
two free valences pointing outwards from the pair of carbon atoms.
Every member of the series carries exactly this group, and the
group decides how the members react. The alkenes are therefore a
**[[homologous-series]]** in the full five-part sense you met in
the introduction to organic chemistry (u4:c22): one functional
group, similar chemical properties, a trend in physical
properties, one general formula, and consecutive members stepping
up by a –CH₂– unit.

The first three members of the family are laid out below — read
the columns the same way you read the alkane table in the previous
lesson.

| Name | Molecular formula | Empirical formula | Structural formula |
|------|-------------------|-------------------|--------------------|
| ethene | C₂H₄ | CH₂ | CH₂=CH₂ |
| propene | C₃H₆ | CH₂ | CH₂=CHCH₃ |
| but-1-ene | C₄H₈ | CH₂ | CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ |

Each molecule can also be drawn as a **[[displayed-formula]]**,
with every bond shown as an explicit line. For ethene that is two
carbon atoms joined by a double line, each carbon also bonded to
two hydrogen atoms by single lines — a flat H₂C=CH₂ arrangement.
Propene adds a –CH₃ group on the second carbon, and but-1-ene
lengthens the chain by one more carbon with the double bond still
between the first two. Drawing these three, and naming the
straight-chain members, is precisely the skill specification
statement 4.26 trains, and Sections 2 and 4 of this lesson drill
it.

Notice one consequence hiding in the table: every alkene has the
same **empirical formula**, CH₂, no matter how big the molecule
gets. That is a direct fingerprint of the double bond — it will be
promoted to the family's general formula in Section 4. Another
consequence sits at the very start of the series: there is no
one-carbon alkene, because a C=C group needs two carbon atoms to
exist. The smallest possible alkene is ethene, full stop.

:::key-point
It is not possible to have an alkene with one carbon atom: alkenes
must contain a C=C group, so a minimum of two carbon atoms is
required. Ethene, C₂H₄, opens the series.
:::

:::prior-knowledge
This chapter assumes the organic-chemistry toolkit from the
introduction (u4:c22) — formula types, homologous series,
functional groups, isomerism — and the alkane family from the
previous lesson (u4:c24), whose saturation gives this chapter its
contrast. The industrial source of the alkenes is cracking, taught
in the crude oil chapter (u4:c23); the covalent double bond itself
was first met in the covalent bonding lesson (u1:c08).
:::

:::cross-curricular
Plant oils are full of alkene-style C=C groups — sunflower oil is
famously polyunsaturated, meaning its molecules carry many of
them. That chemistry leaves the laboratory and lands on the
supermarket shelf: later in this lesson you will meet the
industrial reaction that converts those oils into spreads, the
same reaction food scientists manage every day.
:::

:::exam-hint
When asked what functional group the alkenes contain, write it in
the mark-scheme shape: **the C=C carbon-carbon double bond** (often
written >C=C<). Do not write "a double bond" and leave it there —
say which atoms it joins, because the statement 4.23 wants the
carbon-carbon double bond by name.
:::

:::misconception
"Alkenes and alkanes are both hydrocarbons, so they burn and react
in the same way." The first half is true — both families contain
carbon and hydrogen only — but the conclusion is not. The C=C
functional group makes the alkenes *much more reactive* than the
alkanes: an alkane needs UV light and a substitution mechanism to
react with a halogen, while an alkene attacks bromine instantly
with no conditions at all (Section 7). Same elements, different
bonding, different chemistry.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you state the alkene functional group as a carbon-carbon
double bond? Can you write the molecular formulae of ethene,
propene and but-1-ene, and explain why no one-carbon alkene can
exist? Can you say in one sentence why the family is more reactive
than the alkanes? If all three are yes, move on — the rest of the
chapter is the double bond doing its work.
:::

sections.title: Isomers
sections.markdown:
Once a family reaches four carbon atoms, the double bond starts
generating **[[isomer]]s** — and it generates them in a way the
alkanes never quite did, because the position of the C=C group
becomes a structural variable of its own. Take the molecular
formula C₄H₈. There are two straight-chain alkenes with exactly
these atoms: **but-1-ene**, whose double bond sits between the
first and second carbons (CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃), and **but-2-ene**, whose
double bond sits between the second and third (CH₃CH=CHCH₃). Same
[[molecular-formula]], different structures — the definition of an
[[isomer]] doing its work.

There is also one branched-chain alkene with this formula:
**2-methylpropene**, in which a central carbon carries the double
bond to a CH₂ group and two single bonds to methyl groups — the
CH₂=C(CH₃)₂ arrangement. Drawn as a displayed formula, every one
of the three structures accounts for all eight hydrogens and all
four bonds at each carbon, which is the self-check that keeps
alkene drawing honest: a carbon in a double bond has only two
bonds left for other neighbours, not three.

The naming code decodes exactly as the alkane code did, with one
extra dial. The prefix (but-) counts the longest chain carrying
the double bond; the infix (-ene) announces the double bond; the
number (but-**1**-ene) says *which* carbon the double bond starts
at, numbering from the nearest end. Move the double bond, change
the number, change the compound — but-1-ene and but-2-ene are as
different as two isomers can be, even though their formulae are
identical.

One scope line matters here: with up to four carbon atoms you are
asked to draw the structural and displayed formulae and to name
the **unbranched-chain** isomers — but-1-ene and but-2-ene —
rather than any structure that differs only in the geometry *about*
the double bond. The cis/trans style of labelling is explicitly
not required, so if two drawings of but-2-ene differ only in which
side the end groups sit, treat them as one structure for this
course. Draw the three constitutional isomers of C₄H₈, name the
two unbranched ones, and statement 4.26 is fully served.

:::exam-hint
In "draw the alkene isomers of C₄H₈" items, examiners look for the
double bond *moving*, not just the chain branching. A complete
answer set is but-1-ene, but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene — and each
drawing must show the C=C explicitly. Two structures that differ
only by the geometry about the double bond earn no extra credit:
the course scope excludes that distinction.
:::

:::misconception
"But-1-ene and but-2-ene are the same molecule drawn slightly
differently." They are different compounds: in but-1-ene the
double bond joins carbons 1 and 2, in but-2-ene it joins carbons 2
and 3, so the atoms sit in genuinely different arrangements — the
defining test of an isomer pair. Compare them by asking where the
reactive C=C handle sits, and the difference becomes impossible to
unsee.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you draw and name the two unbranched alkene isomers of C₄H₈
with the double bond in the right place each time? Can you draw
the branched member of the set and check every carbon's four
bonds? Can you state what the number in but-1-ene tells you? Then
you own the isomer skill for this family.
:::

sections.title: Unsaturated hydrocarbons
sections.markdown:
The word *unsaturated* is a classification with a precise bonding
meaning, and the mark scheme pays out only when you give the
bonding version. A **[[saturated-hydrocarbon]]** contains single
carbon-carbon bonds only; an **[[unsaturated-hydrocarbon]]**
contains one or more double or triple carbon-carbon bonds. The
[[alkene]]s are unsaturated compounds *because they contain a C=C
bond* — that causal shape (classification because bonding) is the
sentence specification statement 4.25 asks you to explain, and it
is worth memorising in exactly that order.

A helpful way of thinking about the word is that the alkenes are
*not saturated with hydrogen*: they do not carry the maximum
number of hydrogen atoms possible for their carbon count. An
alkane with two carbons holds six hydrogens; ethene, with the same
two carbons, holds only four — the missing pair is the second
bond between the carbons. The thinking aid is for your
understanding; on its own it is not the definition, and an answer
built only on "they don't have many hydrogens" earns nothing.

The classification also powers a lab skill you will meet in
Section 8: because unsaturated molecules carry a reactive double
bond, they can be told apart from saturated ones with a single
test-tube reagent. Saturation is not just vocabulary — it is a
property you can *detect*. Keep the two definitions paired in your
notes: saturated = single bonds only, unsaturated = at least one
double or triple bond, alkenes = the unsaturated family.

:::key-point
Saturated means single C–C bonds only; unsaturated means the
molecule contains at least one double (or triple) C–C bond. The
alkenes are classified as unsaturated hydrocarbons because they
contain a carbon-carbon double bond.
:::

:::exam-hint
To *explain why alkenes are classified as unsaturated
hydrocarbons*, write the causal sentence: **they contain a C=C
bond** (a carbon-carbon double bond), unlike saturated compounds,
which have only C–C single bonds. A popular thinking aid says
alkenes are "not saturated with hydrogen atoms" — use it only as a
supporting remark after the bonding statement, never as the
answer, because the mark scheme rewards the bonding language.
:::

:::misconception
"Unsaturated means the molecule is missing atoms." It is missing
*hydrogen atoms relative to the maximum* — not missing atoms in
general — and the formal definition says nothing about counts at
all: it is a statement about *bonds* (a C=C is present). Anchor
every unsaturated answer to the double bond and the term can never
slip.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you define saturated and unsaturated in pure bonding language?
Can you explain the alkenes' classification in one causal sentence
with C=C in it? Can you say what a hydrocarbon would need to gain
to turn from unsaturated back to saturated? That last one — two
hydrogen atoms across the double bond — is the bridge to
hydrogenation in Section 9.
:::

sections.title: The general formula
sections.markdown:
The alkane family obeyed CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; the alkene family obeys
**CₙH₂ₙ**. One double bond costs exactly two hydrogen atoms, so the
"plus two" of the alkane formula disappears: an alkene's hydrogen
count is simply **twice** its carbon count. Two carbons carry four
hydrogens (C₂H₄), three carry six (C₃H₆), four carry eight (C₄H₈)
— the [[general-formula]] of statement 4.24, working forwards from
a carbon count to a formula with nothing to memorise per member.

The formula runs backwards too, and the backward direction is the
examinable move. An alkene with 11 carbon atoms must carry
2 × 11 = 22 hydrogen atoms, so its [[molecular-formula]] is
C₁₁H₂₂; handed any candidate formula, divide the hydrogen count by
the carbon count and the family membership question answers
itself — a ratio of exactly two admits the molecule to the alkene
series (with the caveat that ring compounds can mimic the ratio,
a subtlety the question bank likes to probe).

A second consequence flows from the 1:2 ratio: **every alkene has
the same [[empirical-formula]], CH₂**, because that is the
simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms. Ethene, propene,
but-1-ene and C₁₁H₂₂ all reduce to CH₂. If a question asks for the
empirical formula of *any* alkene, the answer is one chip: CH₂ —
no arithmetic required, because the general formula guarantees it.

The same size rule that organised the alkanes organises their
unsaturated cousins. The physical properties of the alkenes are
very similar to those of the alkanes: the small members with up to
four carbon atoms are gases at room temperature, the next dozen or
so are liquids, and the members show the same smooth trend in
properties as the series grows. One general formula, one stepping
unit, one trend — the homologous-series frame doing its job on a
new family.

:::worked-example
An alkene has 11 carbon atoms. What is its molecular formula?
Apply CₙH₂ₙ: hydrogens = 2 × 11 = 22, so the formula is C₁₁H₂₂.
Check: 22 ÷ 11 = exactly 2, so the molecule fits the alkene
pattern — and its empirical formula is CH₂, like every member of
the family. One line of arithmetic, one verification, full marks.
:::

:::exam-hint
Know the two directions of CₙH₂ₙ. Forwards: given 11 carbons,
write C₁₁H₂₂ by doubling. Backwards: given C₆H₁₂, divide 12 by 6,
announce the ratio 2, and claim alkene membership. Questions
typically set one of these two moves, and confusing the alkene
formula with CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ is the single most expensive error in this
topic — the "plus two" belongs to the *alkanes* (u4:c24) only.
:::

:::misconception
"CₙH₂ₙ is the general formula of *organic compounds*." It is the
general formula of the *alkenes* (and, as the question bank
enjoys pointing out, of cycloalkanes — ring-shaped alkane-family
molecules with the same hydrogen ratio). A formula alone never
proves a double bond; the family claim needs the C=C structure,
which is why the bromine-water test of Section 8 exists.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you write the alkene general formula and say what n counts?
Can you produce the molecular formula for the 11-carbon member in
one line? Can you state the empirical formula of every alkene
without computing? Can you place the state boundaries — gases up
to four carbons, liquids beyond? Four yeses and this section is
banked.
:::

sections.title: Combustion
sections.markdown:
Every [[hydrocarbon]] burns, and the [[alkene]]s are no exception:
in air or oxygen they give **carbon dioxide and water** — the same
[[complete-combustion]] products as any other member of the
hydrocarbon club. For ethene the equation is

C₂H₄(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)

Balance-check it once, slowly, because the alkene equations look
slightly odd at first: carbons 2 = 2, hydrogens 4 = 4, and the
oxygens 6 = 2 × 2 + 2 × 1 balance exactly. The odd-looking
coefficient is the 3 in front of O₂ — a consequence of the double
bond leaving *fewer* hydrogens to be turned into water, so the
oxygen splits differently than in an alkane's equation.

What makes this reaction interesting is not the chemistry but the
economics: nobody burns alkenes on purpose. The C=C double bond is
too valuable — it is the reactive handle that lets industry build
alcohols, plastics and dozens of other products, and burning an
alkene simply destroys the handle. Alkanes are cheap fuels;
alkenes are chemical raw materials. That division of labour is why
cracking (u4:c23) is tuned to produce them, and why this chapter's
examinable reactions are the *constructive* ones — addition, not
combustion.

:::did-you-know
The combustion sentence hides an industrial strategy. Refineries
could burn every fraction they make, but the alkene-rich streams
are deliberately saved from the fuel pool: an ethene molecule
converted into ethanol (Section 10) or polythene earns far more
than the same molecule burned in a boiler. Chemistry's version of
"don't spend the seeds".
:::

:::exam-hint
If asked to write the complete-combustion equation of an alkene,
derive it in the fixed order — hydrogens to water first, carbons
second, oxygen last — and you cannot be caught out by the
double-bond stoichiometry. But note the direction of the
specification: statements 4.27 and 4.28 want the *addition*
chemistry, so combustion here is family context, not the
examinable reaction of this chapter.
:::

:::misconception
"Alkenes burn with a smoky flame, so incomplete combustion is
their characteristic reaction." At this level the only combustion
chemistry you need for alkenes is the complete version — carbon
dioxide and water, as for all hydrocarbons. Incomplete-combustion
products (carbon monoxide, soot) belong to the alkanes-and-fuels
story (u4:c23/u4:c24); importing them here muddles two chapters
and earns no marks.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you write the complete-combustion equation of ethene and
balance it in the fixed order? Can you state the two products of
complete combustion for any hydrocarbon? Can you explain in one
sentence why industry avoids burning alkenes? Three yeses and you
have the family context you need.
:::

sections.title: Addition
sections.markdown:
The C=C double bond is the [[functional-group]], and the
functional group determines the chemical properties of a
compound. That is why the [[alkene]]s have characteristic
properties quite different from those of the alkanes — and why
they are much more reactive. The alkane skeleton offers no reactive
handle at all, so alkanes must be bullied into reaction (UV light,
u4:c24); the alkene double bond offers a weak point built into the
molecule, and reagents take advantage of it without ceremony.

That advantage has a name: the **[[addition-reaction]]**. In an
addition, part of the double bond breaks — the two carbon atoms
settle for a single C–C bond — and the electrons that are freed
are used to join *other atoms* onto the two carbons. Two reactant
molecules become **one** product molecule; nothing is ejected,
nothing is swapped. The small molecule simply adds itself across
the double bond, which is why the reaction class is named after
exactly what happens.

Compare the geometry with the substitution you met in the previous
lesson (u4:c24) and the difference becomes visual. Substitution
*replaces* one atom with another and kicks something out
(alkane + Br₂ → halogenoalkane + HBr); addition *consumes* the
double bond and keeps everything (alkene + Br₂ → dibromoalkane,
full stop). Classifier instinct for the rest of organic chemistry:
count the products. One product from two reactants means addition;
two products from two reactants, with an atom exchanged, means
substitution.

The next three sections run the addition cast in full: bromine
(the specification's chosen example), hydrogen (hydrogenation) and
water (hydration). Each follows the same two-step script — break
half the double bond, attach one new atom to each carbon — so
learn the script once and every reagent becomes an instance.

:::key-point
In an addition reaction part of the C=C double bond breaks to
become a single C–C bond, and the freed electrons join other atoms
onto the two carbon atoms. Two molecules become one; the double
bond is consumed.
:::

:::exam-hint
When a question asks you to *describe* an addition reaction, the
mark scheme wants the mechanism sentence and the product count:
**the double bond breaks partially to a single bond, and atoms add
across it, forming one saturated product**. Do not describe the
double bond as "breaking completely" — only half of it breaks; the
C–C link survives, which is precisely why the product is still one
connected molecule.
:::

:::misconception
"Addition and substitution are two names for the same
replacement chemistry." They are different classes with different
product counts: addition turns two molecules into one saturated
product, substitution swaps an atom and produces a small
by-product (HBr in the alkane case). The question bank loves the
contrast — you will meet it head-on in the chapter questions,
where an alkane and an alkene face the same reagent and the
outcomes differ *because* of this distinction.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you define an addition reaction in one sentence with both
halves — double bond partially breaks, atoms add across? Can you
say why alkenes are more reactive than alkanes by pointing at the
functional group? Can you classify a reaction as addition or
substitution by counting products? Then you are ready for the
three named additions.
:::

sections.title: The addition of bromine
sections.markdown:
Bromine adds to [[alkene]]s without any need for heat, light or a
catalyst — the double bond is reactive enough to do the job alone,
which is the sharpest possible contrast with the alkane family,
where bromine refuses to react without ultraviolet light (u4:c24).
In the laboratory the bromine is usually supplied as **bromine
water**, an aqueous solution of the element, and the reaction is
instant on shaking.

With ethene, one bromine atom attaches to each of the two
carbons:

CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br

Drawn as displayed formulae, the equation shows H₂C=CH₂ with its
double line meeting Br—Br, and the single product H—C—C—H carrying
H atoms above and Br atoms below each carbon; the reactants are
labelled ethene and bromine, the product 1,2-dibromoethane. The
structural form says the same thing in compact code: the C=C of
ethene has become C–C, and each carbon gained one Br. That is
[[addition-reaction]] anatomy — two molecules in, one
[[dibromoalkane]] out, no by-product.

The product's name is a naming exercise worth decoding once,
because the decode procedure generalises. **1,2-dibromoethane**:
'eth' shows a two-carbon chain; 'ane' shows only carbon-carbon
single bonds (the double bond is gone — addition saturated it);
'1,2-dibromo' shows two bromine atoms attached to the first and
second carbon atoms. Every dibromoalkane name reports the same
three facts, and reading them back gives you the structure without
drawing anything.

Propene reacts identically — the double bond is the only part of
the molecule doing the work, and the methyl group is a bystander.
Part of the carbon-carbon double bond breaks, two bromine atoms
add across it, and the product is the [[dibromoalkane]]
**1,2-dibromopropane**:

CH₃CH=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₃CHBrCH₂Br

The structure is based on propane, and the prefix '1,2-dibromo'
again reports two bromine atoms on the first and second carbon
atoms — numbering from the end that gives the halogens the lowest
locants, exactly as the naming rules demand. Any compound with a
C=C bond reacts in this same way, which is precisely what makes
the next section's test possible.

:::exam-hint
Two habits pay on every dibromoalkane item. First, decode the
name before drawing: 'eth'/'prop' gives the chain, 'ane' confirms
the double bond is consumed, '1,2-dibromo' places one Br on each
of the first two carbons — then relate the formula you write to
the full displayed structure, because examiners check that the Br
atoms sit *on the carbons*, not floating beside them. Second,
write the product as one molecule: CH₂BrCH₂Br, not
CH₂Br + CH₂Br.
:::

:::misconception
"Alkenes need UV light to react with bromine, like the alkanes
do." That condition belongs to the alkane *substitution* story
(u4:c24) — bromine adds to C=C bonds with no heat, no light and no
catalyst at all. If a question shows bromine reacting in the dark,
that is not a trap: it is the addition pathway, and it is
instantaneous.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you write the ethene-plus-bromine equation in structural form
and name the product? Can you decode 1,2-dibromopropane back into
its structure without hesitation? Can you state the condition
required for bromine to add to an alkene — none? Three yeses and
statement 4.27's chemistry is yours.
:::

sections.title: The test for unsaturated compounds
sections.markdown:
Because *any* compound with a carbon-carbon double bond reacts with
bromine in the same way ethene does, the reaction doubles as a
test. Shake the unknown organic compound with **[[bromine-water]]**
— and if the orange bromine water is decolourised (the colour
changes from orange to colourless), the compound contains a
carbon-carbon double bond. If the unknown is a gas, you do not even
need shaking: bubble it through the bromine water and the same
decolourisation means the same thing. This is the specification's
statement 4.28 — the practical discriminator between an alkane and
an alkene.

Run the test on the two families side by side and the contrast is
the whole point. A liquid alkene shaken with bromine water loses
the orange colour completely, because its C=C bond consumes the
bromine in addition. A liquid alkane shaken the same way keeps the
colour: with no double bond to react, nothing removes the bromine
from the water. Two tubes, one reagent, one observable, zero
ambiguity — which is why this test is a favourite in both
questions and practical work.

:::did-you-know
The comparison has one fine print worth knowing. After shaking an
alkane with bromine water, the colour is not destroyed — it
*moves*: most of the orange ends up in the top organic layer,
because covalent bromine, with its simple molecular structure, is
more soluble in the organic compound than in water. The colour
persistence, not its address, is the diagnostic: in the alkene
tube the colour is gone because the bromine has reacted away, in
the alkane tube it survives because the bromine is untouched.
:::

Mark-scheme language matters here more than usual, because one
word loses marks reliably. The final mixture after a positive test
is **colourless** — not "clear". Clear means not cloudy, see-through;
the bromine water was clear *before* the test, and so is any
ordinary solution. The property that changes is *colour*, orange
to colourless, so write "colourless" and the one mark is safe.

:::exam-hint
Write the test as a three-part sentence and it cannot be
mis-marked: add (or shake with) **bromine water**; the observation
is that it goes **from orange to colourless**; the conclusion is
that the compound is an **[[unsaturated-hydrocarbon]]** — it contains a
C=C bond.
And police the vocabulary: the mixture becomes *colourless*, never
"clear", because clear means not cloudy and was true from the
start.
:::

:::misconception
"Bromine water is a test for alkenes." It is a test for the
**carbon-carbon double bond**, wherever it occurs — any unsaturated
compound decolourises it, not only members of the alkene family.
The distinction matters when the question hands you an unknown: a
positive result licenses "contains C=C", and only with further
evidence (formula, family context) the stronger claim "is an
alkene".
:::

:::quick-check
Can you state the reagent, the colour change and the conclusion of
the unsaturation test in one sentence? Can you say what an alkane
does in the same test and why? Can you explain why "clear" is the
wrong word even though the mixture is see-through? Three yeses and
statement 4.28 is banked.
:::

sections.title: Hydrogenation
sections.markdown:
A **[[hydrogenation]]** reaction is the [[addition-reaction]] in
which the added small molecule is hydrogen: an alkene reacts with
hydrogen, the double bond takes on one H atom at each carbon, and
the product is an [[alkane]]. With ethene:

CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃

Watch the anatomy — it is the same script as the bromine addition,
with a different partner. The C=C becomes C–C; each carbon gains
one hydrogen; two reactant molecules become one product. Ethene
(C₂H₄) becomes ethane (C₂H₆), and the general-formula bookkeeping
confirms it: the product sits in the CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ alkane family, exactly
two hydrogens richer than the alkene it came from. Hydrogenation
is, in other words, the practical answer to the Section 3 closing
question — how does an unsaturated molecule become saturated?

Industry runs this reaction at scale for one household product:
**margarine**. Plant oils — sunflower oil is the classic example —
are *polyunsaturated*, meaning their molecules carry many C=C
groups; that is what keeps them liquid and "oil"-like. Hydrogenate
some of those double bonds and the molecules straighten out and
pack together better, turning the liquid oil into a solid spread.
The degree of hydrogenation is a dial the manufacturer sets:
partially hydrogenated oils stay soft, fully hydrogenated ones go
hard — food chemistry by addition reaction.

:::did-you-know
The same reaction links the supermarket aisle to the chemistry
drawer. "Polyunsaturated" on a label is literally a statement
about C=C bond count — many double bonds per molecule — and it is
why those oils decolourise bromine water vigorously. A drop of
bromine water on sunflower oil would lose its orange colour
faster than on almost any kitchen liquid: the test from Section 8
works on your worktop too.
:::

:::exam-hint
Hydrogenation questions usually want three things: the word
"addition" (classify the reaction), the product family (an
**alkane**, saturated), and the equation with the double bond
consumed. If the question supplies a named alkene — propene, say —
name the alkane product too: propene + hydrogen gives propane.
Never leave the product as "the alkane"; the name is the mark.
:::

:::misconception
"Hydrogenation needs UV light, like the alkane-halogen reaction."
No radiation is part of this reaction's story: hydrogenation is
addition across the reactive C=C, and the double bond needs no
bullying. The UV condition is the *substitution* requirement from
the alkane chapter (u4:c24) — carrying it into addition answers
mixes the two reaction classes the examiner is testing you to
separate.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you define hydrogenation as the addition of hydrogen across a
C=C bond? Can you write the ethene-plus-hydrogen equation and name
the product? Can you explain why polyunsaturated oils harden when
hydrogenated? Three yeses and this addition is yours.
:::

sections.title: Hydration
sections.markdown:
A **[[hydration]]** reaction is the [[addition-reaction]] in which
water adds across the double bond: an alkene reacts with water to
form an **alcohol**. With ethene:

CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH

The script is familiar by now — C=C becomes C–C, one carbon gains
an H, the other gains an –OH — but the conditions are not optional
this time, because water and ethene are not eager partners at room
temperature. In industry the reaction runs with **ethene and
steam** at **300 °C**, a pressure of **60–70 atmospheres** (the
atmosphere is a unit of pressure, equal to 101 325 pascals), and a
**phosphoric acid** [[catalyst]]. Three conditions, one catalyst,
one product: ethanol.

The product is worth naming twice. **[[ethanol]]**, C₂H₅OH, is the
alcohol of the next chapter — and this reaction is precisely how
industry makes high-purity ethanol, with the ethene supplied by
cracking (u4:c23) and the process conditions tuned for yield. The
alcohol family itself — its functional group, its members, its
oxidation chemistry — is the story of a later lesson in this
course (u4:c26); what this section contributes is the *route in*:
the petrochemical industry builds its alcohols from alkene
feedstock by hydration.

As with every addition, the double bond does the deciding.
Hydration of propene would put the –OH on one of two carbons, and
in practice the middle carbon wins: much more propan-2-ol forms
than propan-1-ol, because in the major pathway the hydrogen from
water adds first onto the *end* carbon, leaving the –OH attached
to the middle carbon. The rule governing which way an unsymmetrical
alkene adds is a story for a more advanced level — at IGCSE the
takeaway is simply that the addition goes where the stability is.

:::did-you-know
Hydration is the bridge between two industrial worlds. The ethene
side is petrochemistry: cracking heavy fractions (u4:c23) to make
the small alkene. The ethanol side is everything from solvents to
sanitisers. One reaction — steam, 300 °C, 60–70 atmospheres,
phosphoric acid — is the door between them, which is why the
conditions triplet is one of the most examined condition sets in
the whole organic unit.
:::

:::exam-hint
Learn the hydration conditions as a fixed triplet — **steam,
300 °C, 60–70 atmospheres, phosphoric acid catalyst** — and deploy
them verbatim; "warm with water" earns nothing. If asked to name
the product, say **ethanol** (C₂H₅OH) for ethene. And keep the
reagent word honest: the alkene reacts with *water in the form of
steam* — writing "dilute acid" or "aqueous alkali" signals
confusion with the salts chapter, not hydration.
:::

:::misconception
"Hydration means adding hydrogen, like hydrogenation." One letter,
two different reactions: hydration adds **H–OH** (water) and makes
an alcohol; hydrogenation adds **H–H** (hydrogen) and makes an
alkane. The products differ by exactly one oxygen atom — and by
an entire functional group. Sort the two names now and the
question bank cannot spoof you later.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you write the ethene-plus-steam equation and name the alcohol?
Can you recite the three conditions and the catalyst? Can you say
why the reaction needs forcing conditions when bromine addition
needs none? Can you distinguish hydration from hydrogenation in
one sentence? Four yeses and the final addition is banked.
:::

sections.title: Chapter 25 questions
sections.markdown:
You now hold the complete [[alkene]] story. The family is defined
by its [[functional-group]]-in-waiting — the C=C double bond —
which makes every member an [[unsaturated-hydrocarbon]] (4.25),
gives the family one [[general-formula]], CₙH₂ₙ (4.24), and powers
the [[addition-reaction]]s that consume the double bond: bromine
making dibromoalkanes instantly (4.27), hydrogen saturating the
molecule, water building alcohols under forcing conditions. The
[[isomer]]s of C₄H₈ showed the double bond as a structural variable
(4.26), and the [[bromine-water]] test turned the whole story into
a one-tube experiment (4.28). Every specification statement of
this chapter — 4.23 to 4.28 — has been taught, and each now joins
the platform question bank through the links below, with practice
items keyed to exactly those statements.

Before opening the bank, audit yourself against the chapter's core
moves. Can you explain *unsaturated* in causal bonding language?
Can you run CₙH₂ₙ in both directions? Can you draw the three
alkene isomers of C₄H₈ — and say what a same-formula compound
without a double bond would have to be instead (a ring)? Can you
write all three named addition equations with the products named?
Any wobble is a section to revisit, not a reason to start over.

The question bank for this chapter trains a predictable set of
shapes, so rehearse the moves rather than the answers. Definition
items open the set: the two characteristics of a homologous series
and the unsaturated explanation in exactly Section 3's causal
shape. Test items then hand you a gaseous hydrocarbon that
decolourises bromine water and ask what that observation *tests
for* — C=C, not "alkene-ness" — before demanding the displayed
formula of the three-carbon member and a balanced displayed
equation of its bromine addition. The contrast block sets the same
reagent against an alkane under UV light and asks you to explain
the difference between addition and substitution *using the two
equations* — product counts and consumed versus exchanged atoms
are the currency there. Prediction items close the set: chlorine
onto propene, hydrogen onto ethene, and the triple challenge of
sending but-1-ene at steam, hydrogen chloride and bromine in turn,
naming each product. And the conditions recall from cracking
(u4:c23) returns once more — two conditions for making alkenes,
then a chemical test to tell propane from propene. The shapes are
the chapter; the hydrocarbon names are just costumes.

:::exam-hint
Balance the practice time against the mark structure. Definition
and formula items are fast marks — bank them first. Drawing items
reward the bond-audit habit: every carbon four bonds, the C=C
drawn as a double line, all eight hydrogens placed. Equation items
reward the fixed derive order and named products. For the
addition-versus-substitution explanation, quote both equations and
compare them explicitly — one product with the double bond
consumed, versus an exchange with a by-product — because that
side-by-side is what "using the equations you have already
written" is instructing you to do.
:::

:::misconception
"The question bank rewards knowing the printed answers." It
rewards knowing the *chemistry* — the same addition can be asked
about through a different alkene, a different halogen or a
different small molecule, and a memorised answer to a different
question will not fit. This lesson trained the transferable
routines: the general-formula substitution, the backbone-then-
double-bond drawing audit, the decode-the-name procedure, the
three-part test sentence. Run the method and the costume does not
matter.
:::

:::summary
- **The functional group (4.23)**: alkenes contain the
  carbon-carbon double bond, >C=C<; no one-carbon member can
  exist, because a C=C group needs two carbon atoms.
- **The general formula (4.24)**: CₙH₂ₙ — hydrogens are twice the
  carbons; every alkene's empirical formula is CH₂; the 11-carbon
  member is C₁₁H₂₂; gases up to C₄H₈, liquids beyond, with the
  alkane-like smooth trend in physical properties.
- **Unsaturated (4.25)**: alkenes are classified as unsaturated
  because they contain a C=C bond; saturated compounds carry
  single C–C bonds only.
- **Isomers (4.26)**: C₄H₈ has but-1-ene, but-2-ene and
  2-methylpropene; draw structural and displayed formulae up to
  four carbons and name the unbranched-chain isomers; cis/trans
  labelling is not required.
- **Addition (4.27)**: part of the double bond breaks to a single
  bond and atoms add across it — two molecules become one. Bromine
  adds with no conditions (CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br,
  1,2-dibromoethane; propene gives 1,2-dibromopropane); hydrogen
  gives the alkane (CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃ — hydrogenation, the
  margarine reaction); water/steam gives the alcohol
  (CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH — hydration at 300 °C, 60–70 atm,
  phosphoric acid catalyst, the industrial ethanol route, u4:c26).
- **The test (4.28)**: shake with bromine water — orange to
  **colourless** (never "clear") means C=C; an alkane keeps the
  colour (it just migrates to the organic layer). The reagent
  tests for the double bond, not for a family name.
:::

:::can-you
- state the alkene functional group and explain why no one-carbon
  alkene exists?
- write CₙH₂ₙ, run it forwards (formula from carbons) and backwards
  (membership from formula), and give the empirical formula of any
  alkene?
- define saturated and unsaturated in bonding language and explain
  the alkenes' classification in one causal sentence?
- draw and name the two unbranched alkene isomers of C₄H₈ and the
  one branched member, with every bond accounted for?
- write the three named addition equations — bromine, hydrogen,
  water — with correct products and names?
- decode a dibromoalkane name into its structure and back?
- state the bromine-water test as reagent, colour change and
  conclusion, and explain what an alkane does in the same test?
- recite the hydration conditions triplet and distinguish
  hydration from hydrogenation on sight?
:::

:::quick-check
If every line of the Can-you checklist above is a confident yes,
you are exam-ready on 4.23–4.28 and the platform bank below is
pure consolidation. If any line wobbled, the fix is surgical: jump
back to that section, reread the key-point box, and retry the
worked example — every section in this lesson was built so that a
single weak link can be re-forged without redoing the family.
:::
